en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the female lay follower Kāṇamātā was faithful and confident.
Kāṇā had been given in marriage to a certain man in a village.
Then Kāṇā went to her mother’s house on some business or other.
Then the husband of Kāṇā sent a messenger to Kāṇā, saying: “Let Kāṇā come; I desire Kāṇā’s arrival.
Then the female lay follower Kāṇamātā thought, “How can I go empty-handed? and she baked some cakes.

When the cakes were baked, a certain monk who was wandering for alms entered the residence of the female lay follower Kāṇamātā. Then the female lay follower Kāṇamātā had the monk given some of the cakes.
So, having gone out, he told another; for him too, he had cakes given.
He went out and told yet another; for him too, he had cakes given.
Thus, the cakes that had been prepared came to an end.
A second time, the husband of Kāṇā sent a messenger to Kāṇā, saying, “Let Kāṇā come; I desire Kāṇā’s arrival.
A second time, the female lay follower Kāṇamātā thought, “How can I go empty-handed? and she baked some cakes.
When the cakes were baked, a certain monk who was wandering for alms entered the residence of the female lay follower Kāṇamātā.
Then the female lay follower Kāṇamātā had some cakes given to that bhikkhu.
Having gone out, he told another [bhikkhu]. She had cakes given to him as well.
Having gone out, he told another. She had cakes given to him as well.
The prepared cake was completely consumed.
A third time, the husband of Kaṇā sent a messenger to Kaṇā, saying: “Let Kaṇā come; I desire Kaṇā’s arrival.
If Kaṇā does not come, I shall bring another wife.”
A third time, the female lay follower Kāṇamātā baked cakes, as if she were going away empty-handed.
When the cakes were baked, a certain monk who was wandering for alms entered the residence of the female lay follower Kāṇamātā.
Then the female lay follower Kāṇamātā had the cakes given to that monk.
So, having gone out, he told another; for him also he had cakes given.
He went out and told another; for him also he had cakes given.
Thus the cakes that had been prepared came to an end.
Then the husband of Kāṇā brought another wife home.
Kāṇā heard that “another wife has been brought home by that man,” and she stood there weeping.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, approached the residence of the female lay follower Kāṇamātā; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the female lay follower Kāṇamātā approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she sat down to one side.
As the female lay follower Kāṇamātā was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to her: “Why is this Kāṇā weeping? Then the female lay follower Kāṇamātā informed the Blessed One of the matter.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the female lay follower Kāṇamātā with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat and departed.
Now at that time, a certain caravan was about to set out from Rājagaha for Paṭiyaloka.
A certain alms-collecting bhikkhu entered that caravan for alms.
A certain lay follower had them give roasted flour to that bhikkhu.
So, having gone out, he told another; for him too, she had porridge given.
He went out and told another; for him too, she had porridge given.
Thus, the provisions prepared as travel rations came to exhaustion.
Then that lay follower said this to those men:
“Noble sirs, please wait until tomorrow; the provisions already prepared will be given to you.
I shall prepare further provisions.”
“It is not possible for you to arrive; the caravan has set out,” they said, and so they departed.
Then, as that lay follower was traveling after having prepared provisions for the journey, bandits robbed him.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can these recluses, sons of the Sakyan, accept [food] without knowing moderation?
This person, having given to them, was robbed by bandits while returning later.
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and expressing their indignation.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the bhikkhus:
"In that case, bhikkhus, I will lay down a training rule for the bhikkhus based on ten reasons."
For the well-being of the Saṅgha, for the comfort of the Saṅgha …pe… for the support of the Vinaya.
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:

“If a family has approached a monk and invites him to accept cakes or dough-cakes, a monk who so desires may accept two or three bowlfuls. If he should accept more than that, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).”
"Having accepted two or three bowlfuls, he should then take them out and share them with the other monks. This is the proper conduct in this regard.
Now, regarding the phrase "a family has approached a monk":
"family" refers to four types of families—the khattiya family, the brāhmaṇa family, the vessa family, and the sudda family.
"Upagata" means gone there.
"Pūva" (cake) means—
Whatever is prepared for the purpose of a gift;
"mantha" refers to whatever is prepared for the purpose of provisions for a journey.
"Let him invite [him] by bringing [food]" means:
"Take as much as you wish. "By one who desires" means:
by one who wishes.
"By one who desires.
"Two or three bowlfuls should be accepted" means that two or three bowlfuls should be accepted.
If he should accept more than that:
if he accepts more than that, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Having accepted two or three bowlfuls...
When departing from there, if he sees a monk, he must inform him: “I have accepted two or three bowlfuls over there; do not accept any there.
If he sees one and does not inform him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, after being informed, he nevertheless accepts, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
"Having brought it out from there, it should be shared with the bhikkhus"— meaning that after bringing it out from the place of seclusion, it should be shared.
This is the proper procedure in this matter.
This is the rule of conformity in this case:
if one accepts more than two or three bowlfuls while perceiving it to be more, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one accepts more than two or three bowlfuls while being in doubt, there is an offense of expiation.
If one receives more than two or three bowlfuls while perceiving it to be less, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one receives less than two or three bowlfuls while perceiving it to be more, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one receives less than two or three bowlfuls while being in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is less than two bowlfuls and he perceives it as less,
there is no offense.
There is no offense if he accepts exactly two bowlfuls.
He receives less than two bowlfuls;
they do not give what was prepared for the purpose of a gift or for the purpose of provisions for a journey,
nor do they give the remains of what was prepared for the purpose of a gift or for the purpose of provisions for a journey.
They give when the journey has been brought to rest; [they give] to relatives,
[and] to those who have invited them.
For the sake of another,
with one's own wealth,
[or] for one who is insane.
"For one who is a first offender.
The fourth training rule concerning Kāṇamātā is concluded.
